question: Does historical red tsestá-na provide an independently segmented bridge to modern color -na?

historical_evidence.source: Merrill et al. 2020 analysis of Steffel
historical_evidence.suffix_analysis: -na classified by Merrill as a verbalizer with several functions/bases
historical_evidence.modern_comparison_by_merrill: tsestána ‘es rojo’ || sitána ‘estar rojo; ponerse rojo, enrojecer, ruborizarse’
historical_evidence.phonological_comment: Merrill notes that the historical red forms and their modern equivalents involve loss/addition of unstressed syllables in addition to other possible changes.

modern_multivariety_evidence.source: Compendio básico de la gramática ralámuli, 1997

comparison.functional_match: strong: historical ‘be red’ and modern ‘become/be partially red’ in the same color domain
comparison.independence: high: historical source and modern multivariety elicitation are independent evidence layers

assessment.reason: The same suffixal shape occurs in an explicitly segmented historical red predicate and a systematically described modern color paradigm with closely matching semantics. However, historical -na is a more general verbalizer and modern color -na may represent semantic specialization or retention rather than simple unchanged identity.

relation_to_kame_bridge: This is a second, structurally independent color bridge. The first links historical -kameke~-kame to modern -ka-me in black/white; the present bridge links historical tsestá-na to modern sitá-/setá-/sejtá- + -na.
open_questions: Can the historical root tsestá-/stá- and modern sitá-/setá-/sejtá- be reconstructed through a controlled correspondence series?
Was historical -na already semantically specialized for gradable/inchoative color states, or was its color use one instance of a broader verbalizing function?
Can modern -na in blue/green, black, white and yellow be linked to independent historical color predicates?
